claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is primarily governed by engineered microstructural architecture.
Deliberately designed lamellar or gradient structures create interfaces that impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion delays plastic deformation.
The coatings of interest possess a heterogeneous lamellar or gradient microstructure.
Multilayer interfaces and microstructural heterogeneities act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Multilayer interfaces and microstructural heterogeneities promote localized strain partitioning.
Structured multilayer interfaces obstruct dislocation propagation.
Obstruction of dislocation propagation reduces the strain rate under sustained load.
Obstruction of dislocation propagation delays the onset of plasticity under sustained load.
Engineered multilayer coatings will accumulate plastic strain more slowly than homogeneous high-entropy-alloy coatings under identical conditions.
The proposed behavior applies when dislocation glide, rather than diffusional creep, dominates plastic deformation.
The proposed behavior requires the multilayer interfaces to remain intact.
The magnitude of the interface-barrier effect and the critical dimensions needed to obtain it are not known precisely and may depend on processing conditions.
